the-apple-1998.gazette: The case reached Tehran's newspapers first — twin girls kept inside the family house for most of their lives, released after neighbors signed a petition to the welfare office. Filming began almost immediately, with the father, the mother and both daughters playing themselves on the street where it happened. Event and reconstruction are separated by a matter of days.

the-celebration-1998.gazette: The rules came before the film. Two Danish directors signed a ten-point vow in 1995 — no added light, no mounted camera, no props carried to location — and Vinterberg staged this family reunion inside them, handheld, in whatever the rooms gave him. The certificate issued with the finished picture vouched for how it was made and for nothing else.

the-idiots-1998.gazette: Dogme's second certified film put the vow to its hardest test: von Trier operated the camera himself, worked in available light, and let crew and equipment drift into frame rather than break a rule to keep them out. The performances were staged; certain acts inside them were not. Censors in several countries resolved the difference by blacking out the frame.
the-idiots-1998.prism: The vow promised no artifice, and the film kept that promise in the one place where keeping it costs somebody something. Everything else on the list — the light, the lens, the sound — only ever cost the director.

american-movie-1999.gazette: Chris Smith spent roughly two years in Menomonee Falls, Wisconsin, following Mark Borchardt's attempt to finish a black-and-white horror short called Coven. The production ran on borrowed money, an elderly uncle's savings, and friends who quit and came back. Coven was completed; the documentary about completing it is the film that traveled.

rosetta-1999.gazette: The Dardennes work in and around Seraing, the Walloon steel town where the mills went quiet, and they shoot the way a camera follows a person down a corridor — close behind the shoulder, handheld, no score anywhere. Rosetta wants a job and the film grants her nothing a job would not. Belgium later attached her name to a plan on youth employment.

the-straight-story-1999.gazette: In 1994 a 73-year-old Iowan named Alvin Straight drove a riding lawnmower some 240 miles into Wisconsin to reach a brother he had not spoken to in years. The route, the machine and the reason are all on the record, and Lynch tracked them closely, shooting along the same roads at the same time of year. What the film contributes is the pace, which belongs to the mower.

code-unknown-2000.gazette: Haneke assembled the film from single takes separated by black — each fragment beginning and ending without cushion, the camera fixed or panning once and never cutting to help. The scenes gather in Paris around 2000: a Romanian woman begging on a boulevard, a Malian family in an apartment block, a discarded wrapper that sets the rest in motion. Nothing is scored, and no scene explains the one before it.

o-brother-where-art-thou-2000.gazette: Deakins had a green Mississippi summer to shoot and a Dust Bowl to deliver. Rather than strip the color photochemically, the production scanned the entire picture, graded it digitally and printed it back — the first feature handled that way end to end — until the landscape sat in the dry browns of Walker Evans's photographs. The reference was a government file: images commissioned by the Farm Security Administration in the 1930s to document the same country the film walks across.

the-circle-2000.gazette: A camera picks up one woman in a Tehran street, follows her until she hands off to another, and keeps going. The obstacles are procedural rather than dramatic — a bus ticket that requires a male guardian, a cigarette that cannot be lit in public, a hotel room that cannot be taken alone. The film took the Golden Lion at Venice and was not released in Iran.
the-circle-2000.prism: The walls the women keep hitting aren't plot devices; they're ordinary administrative facts, which is exactly why the film couldn't screen in the country it was shot in. A story can be argued with. A procedure just gets recognized.

yi-yi-2000.gazette: Nearly three hours go to one Taipei family across a wedding, a coma and a funeral, in long takes often framed through glass, so the street keeps appearing in the window of the room. The apartments are ordinary and the office politics are ordinary, and the eight-year-old photographs the backs of people's heads because otherwise nobody sees them. Yang won best director at Cannes; the film never opened in Taiwanese cinemas.

the-experiment-2001.gazette: Stanford, August 1971: paid volunteers were sorted at random into guards and prisoners in a converted basement corridor, and the study was shut down after six days of a scheduled two weeks. Hirschbiegel keeps the design intact — the coin-toss assignment, the uniforms, the escalation — and then carries the final act well past anything the record holds. The experiment ended in a debriefing; the film ends in a body count.

25th-hour-2002.gazette: Benioff's novel predates the attacks; Lee shot the adaptation in New York over the winter that followed and put the city's condition in the frame rather than the dialogue. The credits run over the Tribute in Light, and one long scene plays out at an apartment window above Ground Zero, the excavation still being worked below. It was among the first American features to use the site as a location rather than a subject.
25th-hour-2002.prism: Shooting the pit as a view out a window instead of a plot point means the film never has to state what it thinks about it. The cost is that the city turns into scenery for one man's last night of freedom, and scenery doesn't get to answer back.

bowling-for-columbine-2002.gazette: Moore built the film from material that already existed: the Columbine cafeteria security tapes, news coverage of a six-year-old shooting a classmate near Flint, footage of NRA rallies held close to both towns soon after. It won the Academy Award for documentary feature and has been fought over ever since, almost entirely on questions of sequence — what was cut next to what, and whether one speech was ever one speech. The events are documented. The joins are the argument.

gangs-of-new-york-2002.gazette: Asbury's 1928 chronicle supplied the gangs, the argot and the map of the Five Points; the July 1863 draft riots and Tweed's machine supplied the ending. The neighborhood was rebuilt block by block at Cinecittà in Rome, since nothing of it survives in lower Manhattan. The riots ran four days in life, and the draft they were fighting could be bought out of for three hundred dollars.

oasis-2002.gazette: Lee cast an able-bodied actor as a woman with cerebral palsy and then withheld every softening the role usually receives — no score to carry her scenes, no moment staged to collect sympathy on her behalf. Her counterpart is a man newly out of prison for a hit-and-run he did not commit and cannot explain. Venice gave the film best director and gave her its prize for a young performer; in Seoul the argument was about how the two of them first meet.
oasis-2002.prism: Realism about marginalized people usually buys goodwill early by making everyone likeable. This one spends that credit in the opening minutes, on a scene that leaves the man indefensible, and then keeps him on screen anyway.
